paras: The lynching of Tom McDaniel took place on the night of August 31, 1880, when a band of men took McDaniel, a farmer of about 28, from his sickbed near Commercial Point, Pickaway County, Ohio, and hanged him to a tree near his home. A card on the body signed by a "Vigilance Committee" warned against interference, and an inquest returned a verdict of death by persons unknown. Papers across the country carried the story, many under the name Thomas McDonald, and a Columbus correspondent called it the first lynching in the county's history.

According to the Columbus correspondent who visited the scene, McDaniel had come from Falmouth, Kentucky, as a boy, worked as a farm hand for a large landowner named Decker, and eloped with Decker's daughter Alice. The same account attributed to him years of fights, shootings and threats around Commercial Point, as well as a recent jailing at Circleville for taking a buggy. The wire report described him as "a desperado, quarrelsome and vindictive" and said a feud had existed between him and his neighbors.

On the Monday before his death, McDaniel entered the store of Martin Beaver, a relative of his wife, with a knife and announced he would kill him. Beaver overpowered him and gouged out his one remaining eye, the other having been lost in a hunting accident that spring, and McDaniel was carried home blind.

About 11:30 that night, as his wife was tending his eye, about eight armed men came through the open door and ordered her out of the room. McDaniel asked, "Boys, are you going to kill me?" but received no reply; the men bound his hands, put a halter-rope noose around his neck, and dragged him about 400 yards over a rail fence and through brush to a small red oak by the road, where they hanged him. Passers-by found the nearly naked body the next morning, and a strip of his shirt carried the warning signed "VIGILANCE COMMITTEE".
The Eaton Democrat gave a different picture: twelve disguised men with visors carried him from the house, ran with the rope about 300 yards, and he was believed dead before he reached the tree.

Justice of the Peace Beaver had the body cut down after 8 a.m. and held an inquest, examining the widow and five other witnesses; the verdict was death "by person or persons unknown." McDaniel was buried at 5 o'clock that day, with people coming to the funeral from miles around, and the correspondent reported that no one would guess who had done it and "nobody was sorry." Der Westbote reported that a detective named Nortis had been engaged to find the men but that local people refused to help and threatened him. Only the Eaton Democrat reported that McDaniel's wife recognized one of the men as Satterfield, a township constable, and no report of an arrest or trial appears in the coverage.

A brief Columbus wire dated September 1 ran in papers from Washington and New York to Dakota and Nevada, describing the victim as a desperado but calling the hanging "this horrible murder." The Chicago Tribune printed the correspondent's long account under the headline "A Bit of Red-Oak Justice," and the Wheeling Register and, in November, the Delaware State Journal ("A Human Wolf") reprinted it.

Some papers criticized the killing: the Columbus weekly Der Westbote wrote that his character could not excuse attacking a blind man in bed and that a similar case in the South would have been used for political purposes. The Morristown Gazette in Tennessee made the same point, calling it a "brutal lynching" in Garfield's home state and asking a local paper that criticized Southern lynch law to give it equal attention.

Accounts differ on the number of men, from seven or eight to twelve, and on the hour, from 11 p.m. to 2:30 a.m. They also differ on whether the men were masked: the correspondent said they were not disguised, while the wire, Der Westbote and the Eaton Democrat described masked or disguised men. Most papers called him Thomas McDonald, but the reporter who visited the scene and Der Westbote's correction give his name as Tom or Thomas McDaniel.

reader.title: Lynching of Tom McDaniel
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A band styling itself a 'Vigilance Committee' took McDaniel from his bed and hanged him to a tree (A9, A11, A19).

Seven to twelve men took McDaniel from his house and hanged him without legal process (A11, A14, A16); the card left on the body, signed 'VIGILANCE COMMITTEE', claimed to 'protect all law-abiding citizens' (A11).

Independent accounts (the Columbus wire A2/A4, the correspondent's site visit A9/A11, the Columbus German weekly A15 and the Eaton Democrat A16) agree he was taken from his bed and hanged near his home.

accounts.label: Columbus wire report
accounts.gist: A mob of unknown men took McDonald, a quarrelsome desperado, from his house and hanged him; neighbors were supposed to have done it after his quarrel with Beaver.

accounts.label: Columbus correspondent (site visit)
accounts.gist: About eight armed, undisguised men of a vigilance committee seized the blinded McDaniel at 11:30 p.m., dragged him 400 yards and hanged him, leaving a warning card; the inquest found persons unknown.

accounts.label: Eaton Democrat
accounts.gist: Twelve disguised men with visors carried him out and ran him 300 yards by a halter; he was thought dead before the hanging, and his wife recognized Constable Satterfield.

accounts.label: Der Westbote (Columbus German press)
accounts.gist: Masked men took him at 2:30 a.m.; the follow-up gives seven masked men, a tree 350 yards away, and a detective obstructed by locals.

framing.detail: The wire painted the victim as 'a desperado, quarrelsome and vindictive' yet called the act 'this horrible murder' and 'the outrage'.
The Chicago Tribune's 'A Bit of Red-Oak Justice' detailed his misdeeds at length, called the hanging 'well done', and also described his mutilated body.
Headlines such as 'A Bully Hang to a Tree' and 'A Human Wolf' and descriptions like 'more dangerous than a wild beast' cast him as deserving.
Der Westbote said his character could not excuse the act and that a Southern case would have been used for political ends.
The Morristown Gazette called it a 'brutal lynching' and asked Northern-leaning papers to give it the attention they gave Southern lynchings.

conflicts.note: Der Westbote explicitly corrected McDonald to Thomas McDaniel (A15); the site-visit account uses McDaniel.
The correspondent's account rests on the wife's inquest testimony; the others give no source.
